messages.text: :wave: Hello, team!
Hope you all are doing well
Today I am going to take our first meeting to discuss the project details.
Currently, I have planned all the requirements and overall plan about the software, And i need to share with you about the epics, architecture and tech stack that we need
Lets all see in the meeting to discuss further information.
Hey, sure we can discuss them in the meeting
I will be there

Based on today’s meeting, I have organized the development into three phases.
Phase 1 — Core Task Management
 Phase 2 — Timesheets and Resource Management
 Phase 3 — Prioritization, Risk, and Advanced Features
I have also created the related epics in Jira. We will complete the core workflow first before moving into reporting and advanced features.
Sounds good. Starting with the core workflow first will make the later phases easier to build and test.

For Epic 1, we agreed that the Super Admin will manage the company structure.
The Super Admin can create teams, create users, add members to teams, and assign one Team Lead to each team.
We will use three roles initially: `SUPER_ADMIN`, `TEAM_LEAD`, and `EMPLOYEE`.
Agreed. Those three roles should be enough for the first version.

For authentication, let’s keep the first version simple with username/password login and JWT.
Role-based authorization will be handled in the backend middleware so employees cannot access admin or team-lead endpoints.
We are not adding SSO, email verification, or password reset in this version.
Agreed. JWT with backend role checks is enough for the current scope.

For Epic 2, the Team Lead will create a team goal with a start date and deadline.
Each goal can contain multiple tasks, and every task can be assigned to a team member.
For now, task statuses will be `TODO`, `IN_PROGRESS`, `BLOCKED`, and `DONE`.
Looks good. Keeping the workflow small should be enough for the first release.

One permission rule we agreed on:
Team Leads can create and manage goals and tasks only for their own team.
Employees can see only the tasks assigned to them and can update the status of those tasks.
Agreed. We should enforce that in the backend rather than only hiding things in the UI.

For the first version, goal progress will be calculated from completed tasks.
For example, if a goal has 10 tasks and 6 are completed, progress will show as 60%.
We are not adding weighted task progress yet.
That should be enough. We can improve the progress calculation later if needed.

For Phase 2, employees will be able to log daily time against their assigned tasks.
Each entry will contain the date, hours spent, task, and a short work description.
Employees should not be able to log time against tasks that are not assigned to them.
Agreed. That rule will also keep the resource reports more accurate.

For the duplicate timesheet case, I think we should allow one entry per employee, task, and date.
If the employee submits time again for the same task and date, we update the existing entry instead of creating another one.
For the resource allocation dashboard, we will compare estimated task hours with the employee’s available weekly capacity.

For the simulation, let’s use 40 hours per week.
0–60% = Available
 61–90% = Balanced
 Above 90% = Overloaded
Agreed. Simple thresholds are enough for the first resource dashboard.

For dashboard access:
Team Leads should see only their team’s goals, tasks, timesheets, and resource allocation.
The Super Admin should have a company-level dashboard where all teams can be compared in one view.

For Phase 3, we will introduce task dependencies.
A task can depend on another task, and the system should identify when work is blocked.
We also need to prevent circular dependencies between tasks.

For circular dependency detection, we don’t need anything complex for this scale.
A DFS over the task dependency graph before saving a new dependency should be enough.
If adding the dependency creates a cycle, the API should reject it.

For task recommendations, we agreed to use an explainable scoring model rather than AI or machine learning.
The score will consider:
• Manual priority
• Deadline urgency
• Number of tasks blocked by it
• Goal importance
• Whether the task itself is blocked
Agreed. It is better if the Team Lead can understand exactly why a task is ranked higher.

For the initial scoring rules:
High priority = +30
 Medium = +20
 Low = +10
Due within 2 days = +30
 Due within 7 days = +20
Each downstream task blocked = +10
Currently blocked task = -40
We can tune these values later.
Looks fine for the first implementation. Keeping the weights configurable would be useful.

For the final epic, the risk dashboard should identify deterministic problems instead of predicting risks with AI.
Initial conditions:
• Overdue task
• High-priority blocked task
• Unassigned task
• Goal approaching deadline
• Employee overloaded
• Actual hours exceeding estimate

We should also keep an activity history for important changes.
For V1, let’s record task status changes, assignments, priority changes, and timesheet updates.
We don’t need a complete field-by-field audit system yet.

Architecture decision from the meeting:
Frontend — React + TypeScript
 Backend — Node.js + Express + TypeScript
 Database — PostgreSQL
 ORM — TypeORM
 API — REST
We will keep the backend as a modular monolith.
Agreed. Microservices would add unnecessary complexity for this application.
Also let's go with Cntrollers, services, repositories and entities as architecture of the current running system

Inside the backend, I’m planning to separate the code by domain:
`auth`
 `users`
 `teams`
 `goals`
 `tasks`
 `timesheets`
 `dashboards`
 `audit`
They will remain inside the same application but keep clear module boundaries.

One important scope decision:
For Phase 1, we only need authentication, teams, users, goals, tasks, and assignments.
Timesheets, resource dashboards, task dependencies, and recommendations should not be added until their planned phases.

I have created the six epics in Jira based on these decisions.
I’ll keep the Jira tickets as the source for implementation work, and we can use Slack mainly for requirement clarifications and technical decisions like these.
Sounds good. I’ll refer to the Jira epic when working on each feature.
Thanks to mention all of stuff here
Yeah, no worries, because we all working as a team and we need to communicate well to keep our understanding throughout the development

Today I have completed the Epic 1 — Team and User Administration : <https://kavindaweerasinghe.atlassian.net/browse/TRACKIT-6?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiYmIzMzVmYjI0MDliNDc3OWExMjkyMzMwNzdkMTJiZjgiLCJwIjoiaiJ9|kavindaweerasinghe.atlassian.net/browse/TRACKIT-6?atlOrigin=…>  as the first step of the phrase 1

Also I was able to complete this Epic 2 — Goal, Task, and Assignment Management : <https://kavindaweerasinghe.atlassian.net/browse/TRACKIT-7?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiZjA5MTdhMjI4NDMwNGMyMmJhZTBlYzQ5ZGNkODkyOTEiLCJwIjoiaiJ9|Epic 2 — Goal, Task, and Assignment Management> as well
Great nice work...

But I have made one mistake. I missed epic 1 and 2 are on same phrase and with that i made seperate phrase 1 and 2 readme doc file and committed them. I also made the 2 documentation pages on Confluence

But finally I see the misunderstanding i made and i make new task : <https://kavindaweerasinghe.atlassian.net/browse/TRACKIT-41?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiNGVkMDc4ZjIwNWJkNGE0NTgwYTRkZTllOTZkNmMwZWUiLCJwIjoiaiJ9|Consolidate Epic 1 and Epic 2 into a single Phase 1 end-to-end document> and fixed it
